text.p: One of the defining moments in track and field came in the 1991 world long jump duel between American duo Carl Lewis and Mike Powell.
After a protracted battle, Powell prevailed but needed a world record of 8.95 metres, surpassing Bob Beamon's 23-year-old mark of 8.90 set at the 1968 Olympics.
Six years on Powell's effort in Tokyo still stands as the best long jump ever.
Cuba's Ivan Pedroso, 24, and then the Pan American junior champion, recalls sitting at home in Havana watching the contest.
"I remember it well," he said. "It was the greatest long jump contest I'd ever seen."
In Gothenburg two years ago Pedroso succeeded Powell, the 1991 and 1993 gold medallist, as the world champion. Now he is plans to succeed Powell as the world record holder.
"Nine metres is a reachable target. I feel sure I can do it," Pedroso said. "That is my dream and I think it is possible although it is obviously very difficult to achieve."
Pedroso's ambitions of exploring uncharted territory at the world championships have meant he has restricted his outings in the early part of this outdoor season.
"In Athens I want to be in top shape, to win the title and obtain a good mark."
The Cuban has already briefly experienced life at the top.
He jumped an altitude-assisted 8.96 metres at the Italian ski resort of Sestriere two years ago only for it to be removed from the record books.
The distance was never ratified as the International Amateur Athletic Federation ruled that an official had obstructed the wind gauge.
It is a decision which still angers Pedroso.
"The record was stolen from me. They took away my world record but what can I do against that decision? The only thing to do is to break it again."
Losing the world record is not the only setback Pedroso has endured in the last two years since taking the 1995 world title.
Pedroso was the overwhelming favourite to add an Olympic gold medal to his list of honours.
However a thigh injury early in the 1996 outdoor season required surgery and it is a testament to his toughness that he was able to compete in Atlanta at all.
"I expected to win the Olympic title with a good mark at the start of the season.
"But after I was injured and had the operation I ruled out the possibility of going to the Olympics but I felt good when I started training again.
"I easily gained a spot in the final but my body did not respond on the day. I had not participated in any other competition since the operation."
Pedroso eventually finished 12th in an event where Carl Lewis won his historic fourth consecutive title in his final long jump competition.
Injury denied Pedroso an Olympic title. It also led to his long jump career.
At the age of 12, Pedroso was a promising cross country runner and dreamed of becoming another Alberto Juantorena, the 1976 Olympic 400 and 800 metres gold medallist.
However, a foot problem meant that distance running was too painful a test.
This year, Pedroso has produced a series of outstanding efforts around the European circuit, including a 8.63 metres effort in the Italian city of Padua.
A slight ankle injury sustained while warming up for a meeting in Salamanca, Spain, on July 14 prompted his withdrawal from that competition and the Nice Grand Prix two days later.
Pedroso is confident that he can shrug off his latest setback and go beyond nine metres in Athens.
And he has the endorsement of one man who went very close to beaking that barrier nearly thirty years ago.
"I think Pedroso can go beyond nine metres," Beamon said.
